unresponsive.name: Unresponsive person
immediate_actions: Check that the scene is safe.
Check whether the person responds when you speak and gently tap them.
If they are unresponsive and not breathing normally or only gasping, call your local emergency service and start CPR.
questions: Are they responding to you?
Are they breathing normally?
unresponsive.next_steps: If unresponsive and not breathing normally, use the CPR protocol. If unresponsive but breathing normally, place them in a recovery position if safe and monitor breathing.
unresponsive.escalation: Contact emergency services immediately for unresponsiveness, abnormal breathing, or any life-threatening condition.
avoid: Do not leave an unresponsive person alone.
Do not give food or drink to an unresponsive person.
unresponsive.guide: If the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, treat this as cardiac arrest and begin CPR.

cpr.name: Adult cardiac arrest / CPR
immediate_actions: Call your local emergency service, or send someone to call.
Put the adult on a firm, flat surface if this does not delay compressions.
Place both hands in the center of the chest.
Push hard and fast at 100–120 compressions per minute.
Keep going until the person starts breathing or moving normally, or trained responders take over.
questions: Have emergency services been called?
Is this person an adult or a child/infant?
cpr.next_steps: For children, infants, drowning, overdose, or a collapse caused by breathing problems, dispatcher guidance and trained CPR with breaths may be appropriate.
cpr.escalation: This is a life-threatening emergency. Emergency services should be contacted immediately.
avoid: Do not delay CPR to gather extra information.
Do not stop compressions unnecessarily.
cpr.guide: Hands-only CPR is intended for sudden collapse of a teen or adult when the rescuer is not trained or does not want to give breaths.

choking.name: Choking
immediate_actions: If the person can cough forcefully, encourage them to keep coughing and watch them closely.
If they cannot cough, speak, cry, or breathe, call your local emergency service.
For an adult or child with severe choking: give 5 back blows, then 5 abdominal thrusts, and repeat until the object is expelled or they become unresponsive.
For an infant with severe choking: give 5 back blows, then 5 chest thrusts, and repeat.
If the person becomes unresponsive, lower them to a firm, flat surface and begin CPR.
questions: Is the person an adult/child or an infant?
Can they cough, speak, or breathe?
choking.next_steps: Pregnancy or a body size that prevents abdominal thrusts may require chest thrusts instead. Use dispatcher guidance when available.
choking.escalation: Severe choking is life-threatening. Contact emergency services immediately.
avoid: Do not put your fingers into the mouth unless you can clearly see the object.
Do not hang a choking child upside down.
choking.guide: Choking care differs for adults/children and infants, so age must be established before giving detailed technique.

severe_bleeding.name: Severe bleeding
immediate_actions: Call your local emergency service for life-threatening bleeding.
Press firmly and continuously on the wound with gauze or clean cloth.
Keep steady pressure until bleeding stops or emergency responders take over.
If a life-threatening limb bleed cannot be controlled and a tourniquet is available, use it only if you know how or follow dispatcher guidance.
questions: Is the bleeding still heavy or spurting?
Is the person awake and breathing normally?
severe_bleeding.next_steps: Keep the person warm and stay with them. Monitor breathing and responsiveness.
severe_bleeding.escalation: Heavy, continuous, spurting bleeding or signs of shock require emergency medical care.
avoid: Do not repeatedly lift the dressing to check the wound.
Do not remove an embedded object; apply pressure around it.
severe_bleeding.guide: Direct pressure is the first priority for life-threatening external bleeding.

burns.name: Burn
immediate_actions: Move away from the heat or danger if safe.
Remove clothing or jewelry near the burn only if it is not stuck to the skin.
Cool the burn with clean, cool running water for 5–20 minutes.
Get urgent medical help for deep, large, facial, airway, electrical, chemical, or other serious burns.
questions: Was the burn caused by heat, a chemical, or electricity?
Is the burn on the face/airway or larger than the person's palm?
burns.next_steps: Chemical and electrical burns need special precautions and medical assessment.
burns.escalation: Serious burns, including electrical or chemical burns, require urgent medical assessment.
avoid: Do not apply butter, toothpaste, or other household substances.
Do not remove clothing stuck to the burn.
Do not use ice directly on the burn.
burns.guide: Cooling with clean, cool running water is the basic first-aid step for many thermal burns.

bee_sting.name: Bee/insect sting
immediate_actions: Move away from the insect.
Remove the stinger as quickly as possible if it is still present.
Wash the area with soap and water.
Apply a cold pack wrapped in a thin cloth.
questions: Are you having trouble breathing or swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat?
Do you have a prescribed epinephrine auto-injector?
bee_sting.next_steps: If severe allergic-reaction signs occur, call emergency services and use the person's prescribed epinephrine as directed.
bee_sting.escalation: Breathing difficulty, facial/tongue/throat swelling, shock, or severe allergic reaction requires emergency care.
avoid: Do not ignore worsening breathing or swelling.
Do not delay emergency help while waiting for local swelling to settle.
bee_sting.guide: Watch for signs of anaphylaxis because insect stings can trigger life-threatening allergic reactions.

anaphylaxis.name: Severe allergic reaction / anaphylaxis
immediate_actions: Call your local emergency service now.
If the person has a prescribed epinephrine auto-injector, help them use it as directed.
Keep monitoring breathing and responsiveness.
Stay with the person until emergency help arrives.
questions: Is the person having trouble breathing or becoming less responsive?
Is a prescribed epinephrine auto-injector available?
anaphylaxis.next_steps: Use emergency dispatcher guidance and follow the person's prescribed medication instructions.
anaphylaxis.escalation: Suspected anaphylaxis is a life-threatening emergency.
avoid: Do not rely on antihistamines alone for airway or breathing problems.
Do not leave the person alone.
anaphylaxis.guide: Anaphylaxis can worsen quickly and needs emergency treatment.

seizure.name: Seizure
immediate_actions: Move nearby dangerous objects away.
Do not hold the person down.
Do not put anything in their mouth.
Time the seizure and monitor breathing.
When the seizure ends, place them on their side if safe and monitor them.
questions: Has the seizure lasted 5 minutes or longer?
Is this their first seizure, or have they had repeated seizures without recovering?
seizure.next_steps: Emergency care is needed for prolonged/repeated seizures, first seizures, serious injury, seizure in water, or breathing problems.
seizure.escalation: Call emergency services for a seizure lasting more than 5 minutes, repeated seizures, first seizure, serious injury, seizure in water, or breathing problems.
avoid: Do not restrain the person.
Do not put objects, food, water, or medicine in their mouth during the seizure.
seizure.guide: Protect from injury, let the seizure run its course, monitor breathing, and use recovery position afterward when safe.

stroke.name: Possible stroke
immediate_actions: Call your local emergency service immediately.
Note the time the symptoms started, or the last time the person was known to be well.
Keep the person safe and with you.
Do not give food or drink.
questions: When did the symptoms start, or when were they last known to be well?
Is there sudden face drooping, arm weakness, or speech difficulty?
stroke.next_steps: Follow emergency dispatcher instructions and keep monitoring the person.
stroke.escalation: Suspected stroke is time-sensitive and requires immediate emergency evaluation.
avoid: Do not wait for symptoms to improve.
Do not give food or drink while swallowing may be affected.
stroke.guide: Use FAST-type warning signs and treat suspected stroke as an emergency.

chest_pain.name: Chest pain / possible heart attack
red_flags: pain spreading to arm or jaw
immediate_actions: Stop activity and have the person rest in a comfortable position.
Call your local emergency service for severe, persistent, or concerning chest pain.
Stay with the person and monitor breathing and responsiveness.
If they become unresponsive and are not breathing normally, start CPR.
questions: Is the chest pain severe, persistent, or associated with breathing difficulty, fainting, sweating, or pain spreading to the arm/jaw?
Is the person responsive and breathing normally?
chest_pain.next_steps: Emergency dispatchers can guide next steps. Do not delay emergency contact to collect a detailed history.
chest_pain.escalation: Severe or concerning chest pain requires urgent medical evaluation.
avoid: Do not drive yourself if emergency transport is available.
Do not delay emergency help because symptoms seem mild at first.
chest_pain.guide: Chest pain can have serious causes and cannot be safely diagnosed by the app.

breathing_difficulty.name: Breathing difficulty
immediate_actions: Call your local emergency service if breathing is severe or worsening.
Help the person sit in a position that makes breathing easier.
Stay with them and monitor responsiveness and breathing.
If they have a prescribed rescue medicine, help them use it as directed.
questions: Can they speak in full sentences?
Are they becoming blue, confused, very drowsy, or unable to breathe normally?
breathing_difficulty.next_steps: Severe breathing difficulty is an emergency; follow dispatcher guidance.
breathing_difficulty.escalation: Severe or worsening breathing difficulty requires emergency medical care.
avoid: Do not make the person lie flat if that makes breathing harder.
Do not give someone else’s medication.
breathing_difficulty.guide: Breathing problems can deteriorate quickly; prioritize emergency assessment when severe.

fainting.name: Fainting
immediate_actions: Check responsiveness and breathing.
If they are not breathing normally, call emergency services and start CPR.
If they are breathing normally and have recovered, keep them lying or seated safely and monitor them.
questions: Are they awake and responding normally now?
Did they have chest pain, breathing difficulty, serious injury, or repeated fainting?
fainting.next_steps: Seek urgent medical assessment when fainting is unexplained, repeated, associated with injury, or accompanied by serious symptoms.
fainting.escalation: Unresponsiveness, abnormal breathing, chest pain, severe injury, or repeated fainting requires urgent emergency assessment.
avoid: Do not give food or drink until the person is fully alert.
Do not let them stand suddenly if they feel faint.
fainting.guide: The priority is to check responsiveness and breathing and identify emergency warning signs.

fracture_injury.name: Fracture / serious limb injury
immediate_actions: Keep the injured area as still as possible.
Do not try to straighten a deformed limb.
If there is severe bleeding, control it with direct pressure around the wound.
Get urgent medical care for suspected fracture, major trauma, or circulation/sensation changes.
questions: Is there severe bleeding or an open wound over the injury?
Is the limb numb, pale, blue, or unusually cold?
fracture_injury.next_steps: Emergency assessment is especially important after major trauma or when circulation/sensation is abnormal.
fracture_injury.escalation: Major trauma, open fracture, uncontrolled bleeding, or loss of circulation/sensation requires emergency care.
avoid: Do not straighten or force the limb into place.
Do not move someone with suspected spinal injury unless necessary for immediate safety.
fracture_injury.guide: Immobilization and professional assessment are more important than trying to realign an injured limb.

poisoning.name: Possible poisoning
immediate_actions: Move away from the source if it is unsafe to stay nearby.
Call your local emergency service or poison service if available.
Keep the container, label, or substance information available for responders.
If the person is unconscious, having a seizure, or having trouble breathing, treat it as an emergency.
questions: What substance was involved, and roughly how much?
Is the person awake and breathing normally?
poisoning.next_steps: Follow emergency or poison-service instructions. Do not induce vomiting unless a qualified professional specifically tells you to.
poisoning.escalation: Breathing problems, seizures, severe symptoms, or altered responsiveness require immediate emergency care.
avoid: Do not induce vomiting unless specifically instructed by a qualified poison professional.
Do not give food, drink, or a home remedy unless instructed.
poisoning.guide: Poisoning management depends on the substance and exposure route; professional poison/emergency guidance is essential.

heat_illness.name: Heat illness
immediate_actions: Move the person to a cooler place.
Loosen or remove unnecessary clothing.
Cool the person with cool water, wet cloths, or other safe cooling methods.
If they are confused, unresponsive, or having a seizure, call emergency services immediately.
questions: Are they confused, fainting, having a seizure, or difficult to wake?
Can they drink safely and respond normally?
heat_illness.next_steps: Heat stroke is a medical emergency; continue active cooling while awaiting emergency help.
heat_illness.escalation: Altered mental status, seizure, or unresponsiveness with heat exposure requires emergency care.
avoid: Do not leave a severely overheated person alone.
Do not delay emergency care for suspected heat stroke.
heat_illness.guide: Rapid cooling and emergency assessment are priorities when mental status is affected.

electric_shock.name: Electric shock
immediate_actions: Do not touch the person until the electrical source is safely switched off.
Call your local emergency service for significant electrical exposure.
Once the source is off and the scene is safe, check responsiveness and breathing.
If they are not breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available.
questions: Has the power source definitely been switched off?
Is the person awake and breathing normally?
electric_shock.next_steps: Electrical injuries can cause internal injury even when skin damage looks small; medical assessment is important.
electric_shock.escalation: Unresponsiveness, abnormal breathing, burns, or significant electrical exposure requires emergency care.
avoid: Do not touch a person who may still be in contact with a live electrical source.
Do not approach fallen power lines.
electric_shock.guide: Scene safety comes first because rescuers can also be injured by live electricity.

nosebleed.name: Nosebleed
immediate_actions: Sit upright and lean slightly forward.
Pinch the soft part of the nose continuously for 10–15 minutes.
Keep breathing through the mouth while holding pressure.
questions: Has the bleeding continued despite 15 minutes of firm pressure?
Was there a significant head or facial injury?
nosebleed.next_steps: Seek professional care for severe/gushing bleeding, head or neck injury, or bleeding that does not stop after 15 minutes.
nosebleed.escalation: Severe bleeding, significant trauma, or persistent bleeding requires medical assessment.
avoid: Do not tilt the head backward.
Do not repeatedly release pressure to check too early.
nosebleed.guide: Leaning forward helps prevent blood from pooling in the throat.

minor_cut.name: Minor cut / wound
immediate_actions: Wash your hands if possible.
Apply gentle direct pressure with clean gauze or cloth if it is bleeding.
Once controlled, rinse the wound with clean running water and cover it with a clean dressing.
questions: Is the bleeding heavy or still not stopping with direct pressure?
Is the wound deep, gaping, or caused by a bite or dirty/puncturing object?
minor_cut.next_steps: Seek medical care for deep wounds, uncontrolled bleeding, bites, embedded objects, or signs of infection.
minor_cut.escalation: Heavy bleeding or a deep/complex wound needs professional care.
avoid: Do not remove deeply embedded objects yourself.
Do not ignore worsening redness, swelling, pain, or pus.
minor_cut.guide: Simple wounds can often be cleaned and covered after bleeding is controlled.

eye_injury.name: Eye injury
immediate_actions: Do not rub the eye.
If a chemical entered the eye, begin flushing with clean running water immediately and continue while seeking emergency help.
For a visible loose particle, allow tears/blinking to wash it out; do not forcefully remove embedded objects.
Seek urgent medical care for vision loss, severe pain, chemical exposure, or penetrating injury.
questions: Was a chemical or sharp object involved?
Is vision reduced or is there severe eye pain?
eye_injury.next_steps: Chemical eye exposure needs immediate prolonged irrigation and urgent medical evaluation.
eye_injury.escalation: Chemical exposure, penetrating injury, vision loss, or severe pain requires urgent care.
avoid: Do not rub the eye.
Do not pull out an embedded object.
eye_injury.guide: Eye injuries can threaten vision; chemical exposure should be treated immediately.

sprain.name: Sprain / strain
immediate_actions: Stop the activity and protect the injured area.
Rest it and avoid movements that increase pain.
Use a wrapped cold pack for short periods to reduce pain or swelling.
Get medical assessment if there is deformity, severe pain, numbness, or inability to use the limb.
questions: Is the limb deformed, numb, blue/pale, or impossible to use?
Was there major trauma?
sprain.next_steps: A suspected fracture or circulation/sensation problem needs medical assessment.
sprain.escalation: Deformity, major trauma, loss of sensation/circulation, or severe pain requires professional assessment.
avoid: Do not forcefully move or straighten a painful/deformed limb.
sprain.guide: Protect the injury and seek assessment when symptoms suggest more than a simple sprain.
